title: MBAT Club Datathon 2026 — Participant Manual
text:
Welcome
This is the participant manual for the MBAt Club Datathon 2026 (Econometrics and Business Statistics), held Monday 21 – Tuesday 22 September at Learning and Teaching Building, Clayton campus.
It’s a reference to work through before the event and to keep open during the event — you’re not expected to read it cover to cover in one sitting, but every chapter should make sense as a standalone lookup when you’re stuck on something specific.

title: MBAT Club Datathon 2026 — Participant Manual
text:
How to use this manual

1  Code of Conduct — the standards of behaviour we expect from everyone at the event, and how to report a concern.
2  Git + GitHub Desktop — your team’s submission is a public GitHub repository, so this is the one chapter everyone on the team should be comfortable with before Day 1.
3  Quarto — how to write and render the reproducible report and the presentation slides your submission requires — both are mandatory, not just for finalists.
4  Using the Starter Template — the folder layout your team’s repository starts from, and how to fill in and render it.
5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians and 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis — the competition dataset lives in a MongoDB Atlas cluster; these two chapters cover the concepts and the hands-on connection guide for pulling it into R.
8  Resources for tidytext (Text Mining with R) — further reading and techniques for text mining the (mostly free-text) dataset, beyond what’s already worked through in the MongoDB chapter.
9  Good Visualisation & Tables — turning your analysis into a figure or table a judge can actually read at a glance: choosing the right chart, designing for perception, and building a communicative table from a fitted model.

title: MBAT Club Datathon 2026 — Participant Manual
text:
Before you arrive

Install R, RStudio (or Positron/VS Code with the R extension), Quarto, and GitHub Desktop.
Create a GitHub account if you don’t already have one, and share your username with organisers — they create and share your team’s repository, so you just need to clone it (2  Git + GitHub Desktop).
Skim 2  Git + GitHub Desktop and 3  Quarto ahead of time — Day 1 morning is registration, opening remarks, and the dataset introduction, and the working session doesn’t start until 10:30 AM, so setup issues are much cheaper to fix beforehand than mid-competition.

title: MBAT Club Datathon 2026 — Participant Manual
text:
Getting help on the day
A help desk is staffed for the full duration of both days. If you’re stuck on something in this manual for more than a few minutes, ask rather than losing working time to it.

title: 1  Code of Conduct
text:
We are committed to providing a safe, inclusive, welcoming, and harassment-free experience for everyone.
We try to cultivate a community with shared values, where people are comfortable exploring ideas, asking questions, and saying things like “I don’t understand” or “why”. Assume competence in the people you interact with. There are no stupid questions.
Be considerate in speech and actions, and actively seek to acknowledge and respect the boundaries of fellow participants.
Take care of each other. Alert a member of the Code of Conduct Committee (named below) if you notice a dangerous situation, someone in distress, or a potential violation of this Code of Conduct, even if it seems inconsequential.
We do not tolerate harassment in any form. Refrain from demeaning, discriminatory, or harassing behavior and speech. Harassment includes, but is not limited to:

offensive comments related to gender, gender identity and expression, age, sexual orientation, disability, physical appearance, body size, race, ethnicity, religion (or lack thereof), or technology choices
unwelcome comments regarding a person’s lifestyle choices and practices, including those related to food, health, parenting, drugs, or employment
sustained or willful disruption of discussions, talks, or other events
deliberate intimidation
continued one-on-one communication after requests to cease
unwanted photography or recording, including logging online activity for harassment purposes
pattern of inappropriate social contact, such as requesting/assuming inappropriate levels of intimacy with others
inappropriate physical contact without consent or after a request to stop
stalking or following
threats of violence or incitement of violence towards any individual, including encouraging a person to commit suicide or to engage in self-harm
use of sexual or discriminatory imagery, comments, or jokes
unwelcome sexual attention
deliberate “outing” of any aspect of a person’s identity without their consent except as necessary to protect vulnerable people from intentional abuse
deliberate misgendering or use of “dead” or rejected names
publication of non-harassing private communication

This Code of Conduct applies to all people participating in the event, including staff and leadership. It applies to all modes of interaction online including GitHub project repositories, including social gatherings affiliated with the event.
Reporting Guidelines The Code of Conduct Committee includes

Krisanat Anukarnsakulchularp
Janith Wanniarachchi
Maliny Po

If you experience or witness unacceptable behavior, or have any other concerns, please submit a report to the Committee as soon as possible on mbat-ebs@monash.edu. You may also make a report directly to one member of the Committee by contacting them directly. If any member of the Committee has a conflict of interest with a report, they will be recused and will not have access to the content or process of the report followup.
The Code of Conduct Committee will investigate and decide responses to reports with the aim of making a decision and implementing enforcement as soon as is reasonably possible. We are committed to transparency with our community while upholding the privacy of victims.
We welcome your feedback and thank you for working with us to make rOpenSci a safe, enjoyable, friendly and enriching experience for everyone who participates.
This Code of Conducted is adapted from those used by ropensci.org and OceaniaR Hackathon 2025

title: 2  Git + GitHub Desktop
text:
2.1 The daily loop
Everything below is a variation on this:

title: 2  Git + GitHub Desktop
text:
Pull the latest changes.
Do some work.
Commit with a short message.
Push so your team can see it.

title: 2  Git + GitHub Desktop
text:
2.2 Install (before the event)

Install GitHub Desktop.
Sign in with a GitHub account (create one first if needed).
Let it install Git automatically if prompted.
Make sure organisers have your GitHub username so you can be added to your team’s repository.

title: 2  Git + GitHub Desktop
text:
2.3 Get your team’s repository
Organisers create and share one repository per team, already set up from the starter template (Chapter 4) — you don’t create anything.

Get the repo link from organisers.
Every team member: GitHub Desktop → File → Clone Repository → paste the URL → Clone.
Before the working session starts, confirm you can push: make a trivial commit (e.g. add your name to the README) and push it.

title: 2  Git + GitHub Desktop
text:
2.4 Work session workflow

Click Fetch origin, then Pull origin if you’re behind — do this before you edit anything.
Edit your files as normal.
Check the Changes tab — untick anything you didn’t mean to include.
Write a short summary → Commit to main.
Click Push origin.
Repeat: pull → work → commit → push.

Commit often — every working chunk of progress, not just once at the end of the day.

title: 2  Git + GitHub Desktop
text:
2.5 Avoid stepping on your teammates

Split work by file/section so two people aren’t editing the same lines at once.
Pull before you start a session; push before you take a break.
Say out loud (or in chat) before editing a shared file, e.g. the report.

title: 2  Git + GitHub Desktop
text:
2.6 Fix a merge conflict

Open the file GitHub Desktop flags as conflicted.
Find the marked sections:
<<<<<<< HEAD
your version
=======
their version
>>>>>>> branch-name
Edit the file to keep the correct content (or merge both).
Delete the <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> marker lines.
Save, then commit the resolved file as usual.
Stuck for more than a few minutes? Ask the help desk.

title: 2  Git + GitHub Desktop
text:
2.7 Never commit these

Credentials — MongoDB connection string, API keys, .Renviron contents. Keep them in a local .Renviron file, listed in .gitignore.
Large raw data dumps — pull from the database at analysis time instead.
Cache/temp folders — .quarto/, *_cache/. (_docs/ is the exception — see Chapter 4: that one does need to be pushed, since it’s your submitted report and slides.)

If a credential is ever pushed by accident, rotate it immediately — deleting the file does not remove it from the repo’s history.

title: 2  Git + GitHub Desktop
text:
2.8 Prefer the command line?
git clone <repo-url>
git status
git add <file>            # or `git add .`
git commit -m "message"
git pull
git push
Same repository either way — teammates can mix GitHub Desktop and the terminal freely.

title: 2  Git + GitHub Desktop
text:
2.9 Before you submit (Day 2, 11:00 AM deadline)

The final commit is pushed — an unpushed commit does not count as submitted
No credentials appear anywhere in the repo, including old commits
Both the rendered HTML and PDF reports open correctly from a fresh clone
The presentation slides (Chapter 3) are finished and rendered — required from every team, not just finalists

title: 3  Quarto
text:
3.1 Anatomy of a .qmd file
The starter template (Chapter 4) already includes both: docs/report.qmd for the written report and docs/slides.qmd for presentation slides.

title: 3  Quarto
text:
---
title: "Team Name — Datathon Submission"
author: "Team Name"
format: html
---

# Introduction

We analyse the AI Incident Database to answer...

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
summary(cars)
```

Text outside code chunks is normal Markdown.
Anything inside ```{r} ``` blocks runs at render time.
Add #| echo: false inside a chunk to keep the output but hide the code — useful for staying within a word limit.

title: 3  Quarto
text:
3.2 Render your report

RStudio/Positron: click Render, or press Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+K.
Command line:
quarto render report.qmd            # render using the format in the YAML
quarto render report.qmd --to pdf   # force a specific format
quarto preview report.qmd           # live preview, reloads on save

Use quarto preview while you write — it catches broken chunks immediately instead of at the end.

title: 3  Quarto
text:
3.3 Set your output format
Both HTML and PDF are required for the report — list both formats in the YAML and Quarto renders one file for each:
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: true   # readers can expand/collapse code blocks
  pdf:
    documentclass: article
quarto render report.qmd   # produces report.html and report.pdf
The report has a 3,000-word limit, excluding code, tables, figure captions, and references.

title: 3  Quarto
section: 3.4 Build presentation slides (required from every team)
text:
3.4 Build presentation slides (required from every team)
A finished slide deck is part of your submission, not an optional extra — every team builds one, even though only the 5 finalists actually present it live (2:15–3:30 PM, Day 2: 10 min talk + 5 min Q&A each). Treat it with the same care as the report: it’s judged on Professional Communication just like everything else you submit.
---
title: "Team Name — Datathon Presentation"
format: revealjs
---

Start each new slide with a ## heading.
Write R chunks exactly as you would in the report — plots and tables render live into the deck.
Render the same way: Render button, Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+K, or quarto render slides.qmd.
Open the resulting .html in a browser; press f for fullscreen, use arrow keys or space to advance.

## Introduction

The question we investigated...

## Our Approach

```{r}
ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
```

## Results

Key finding...

title: 3  Quarto
section: 3.5 Set up PDF rendering (before the event)
text:
3.5 Set up PDF rendering (before the event)
Since PDF is a required output, don’t leave this until Day 2. PDF needs LaTeX — install it once, ahead of time:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
Render both formats and open both files before the deadline — a report that renders fine to HTML can still fail on PDF (e.g. an image or table that doesn’t fit the page).

title: 3  Quarto
section: 3.6 Keep the report reproducible and inside the word limit
text:
3.6 Keep the report reproducible and inside the word limit

Render early and often — don’t wait until the deadline to find a broken chunk.
Decide how much code you want visible in the final report — the echo, warning, and message options (set per chunk, or globally under execute: in the YAML) control this. There’s no required setup here; choose whatever makes your report read cleanly.
Cache slow steps (a MongoDB pull, a model fit) with #| cache: true on that chunk.
Use knitr::kable() or gt for tables, and pipe large printed output through head() — raw tibble/model printouts can quietly blow out your word count.
Keep the raw .qmd in your GitHub repo, not just the rendered file — the repo is what gets checked for reproducibility.

title: 3  Quarto
text:
3.7 Learn more

<startr.numbat.space> — the club’s starting point for Quarto.
https://quarto.org/docs/guide/ — official docs, every format and option.
quarto --help on the command line, or ?quarto::quarto_render in R.

Stuck on a YAML typo for more than a few minutes? Ask the help desk.

title: 4  Using the Starter Template
text:
4.1 Folder structure
Following this layout isn’t mandatory, but it’s what lets organisers find your work quickly — worth it for the Professional Communication judging pillar.

title: 4  Using the Starter Template
text:
src/ — your R script files. Ships with main.R, which stubs out a connect_to_db() function for you to implement.
data/ — intermediate computed datasets you save as you go.
docs/ — your Quarto files: report.qmd (written report) and slides.qmd (presentation) — see Chapter 3.
_docs/ — generated automatically when you render (set as the output-dir in _quarto.yml). This holds your final rendered report and slides — commit and push it, since it’s what organisers see.
manual/ — reference material from organisers.

title: 4  Using the Starter Template
text:
4.2 Get set up

Clone your team’s repo (Chapter 2).
Open it in RStudio/Positron.
Install the packages the template uses: dplyr, mongolite, here.
Open src/main.R and implement connect_to_db() using your Atlas connection string (Chapter 6) — read it with Sys.getenv(), never hardcode it.

title: 4  Using the Starter Template
text:
4.3 Use your script from a .qmd
Don’t copy-paste code between src/main.R and your .qmd files — source it instead. docs/report.qmd already does this at the top:
source(here::here("src/main.R"))
here::here() keeps file paths working no matter which file you render from — always reference files this way rather than relative paths like "../src/main.R".
For more selective imports, box::use() is also available if you’re already familiar with it — optional, not required.

title: 4  Using the Starter Template
section: 4.4 Fill in the report and slides
text:
4.4 Fill in the report and slides

docs/report.qmd — starts as format: html only. Both HTML and PDF are required, so add a pdf: entry to the YAML before you submit (Chapter 3 shows the format block and PDF setup). Set your team name in the title too.
docs/slides.qmd — already set to format: revealjs. A finished deck is required from every team, not just finalists — only the 5 finalists present it live, but everyone submits one (Chapter 3 covers building slides).

title: 4  Using the Starter Template
text:
4.5 Render everything
From the project root:
quarto render
This renders every .qmd under docs/ and writes the output into _docs/.

title: 4  Using the Starter Template
text:
4.6 Submit
There’s no file to zip or upload — organisers submit by cloning your repository directly.

Run quarto render so _docs/ is up to date.
Commit and push everything, including _docs/ (Chapter 2) — unlike a typical build folder, this one needs to be pushed, since it’s your actual submitted report and slides.
Confirm the repo is public and the final push landed before the deadline.

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
text:
5.1 1. Why This Tutorial Exists
Already comfortable with SQL vs. NoSQL? Skip straight to Chapter 6 and test your connection before the event starts — see its “Common pitfalls” section on network/allow-listing issues.
Written for readers comfortable with R, data frames, and relational databases (SQL, normalized tables, joins).
If you’ve spent time with relational databases, your mental model of data storage is probably something like this:
This model maps naturally onto how you already think about data as a statistician: a rectangular data frame, one row per observation, one column per variable, merge() or dplyr::left_join() to combine data frames.
NoSQL databases (of which MongoDB is the most popular example) relax or abandon several of these assumptions. Understanding why they do this, and what you gain and lose, is the goal of this tutorial.
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
text:
Data lives in tables with a fixed schema (columns defined in advance, with types).
Rows relate to each other through foreign keys, and you stitch related data back together with joins.
You enforce consistency using constraints (primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL, etc.).
A single logical “thing” — like a customer with multiple orders — is normalized across several tables to avoid duplication.
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
text:
5.2 2. What “NoSQL” Actually Means
“NoSQL” is a loose umbrella term (sometimes glossed as “Not Only SQL”) covering several different data models that don’t follow the relational (table-and-join) paradigm. The major families are:








Type
Data model
Example systems




Document
Semi-structured documents (JSON-like)
MongoDB, CouchDB


Key-value
Simple key → value lookups
Redis, DynamoDB


Wide-column
Sparse, column-family tables
Cassandra, HBase


Graph
Nodes and edges
Neo4j, ArangoDB



This tutorial focuses on document stores, and specifically MongoDB, because they’re the most common entry point and the comparison to relational tables is the most direct.
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
section: 5.3 3. The Core Idea: Documents Instead of Rows
text:
5.3 3. The Core Idea: Documents Instead of Rows






WarningThe data used in this example



The examples used in this page are not reflective of the actual data you will use in the competition! They are only presented to get an understanding of the functionalities.


In a relational database, a customer and their orders might be split across two tables:
-- customers table
customer_id | name    | email
------------|---------|------------------
1           | Alice   | alice@email.com

-- orders table
order_id | customer_id | item      | amount
---------|-------------|-----------|-------
101      | 1           | Widget    | 9.99
102      | 1           | Gadget    | 19.99
To get “Alice and all her orders,” you JOIN on customer_id.
In MongoDB, you’d likely store this as a single document:
{
  "_id": "1",
  "name": "Alice",
  "email": "alice@email.com",
  "orders": [
    { "item": "Widget", "amount": 9.99 },
    { "item": "Gadget", "amount": 19.99 }
  ]
}
A “document” is essentially a JSON object (technically stored as BSON, a binary superset of JSON with extra types like dates and integers). Documents are grouped into collections, which are the loose analogue of tables — except a collection has no fixed schema. Two documents in the same collection can have completely different fields.

5.3.1 A translation table for vocabulary







Relational term
MongoDB term




Database
Database


Table
Collection


Row
Document


Column
Field


Primary key
_id field


Join
Embedding, or $lookup (an actual join-like operation)


Schema (rigid)
Schema (optional / flexible)
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
text:
5.4 4. Why Embed Instead of Normalize?
This is the conceptual heart of the difference, and it’s worth dwelling on because it inverts a habit that’s deeply ingrained if you’ve learned relational design.
Relational design philosophy: normalize aggressively. Store each fact once. Avoid redundancy. Joins are cheap(-ish) and consistency matters more than read speed.
Document design philosophy: model around your access patterns. If you almost always fetch a customer along with their orders together, store them together, even if that means the word “Widget” is duplicated across many documents. Reads become a single lookup instead of a join across multiple tables — this matters a lot for web-application workloads with high read volume and simple, predictable query shapes.
The tradeoff: - Relational: harder to scale horizontally, but strong guarantees around consistency and no duplicated data to keep in sync. - Document: easier to scale horizontally and often faster for “fetch this one entity and everything about it” queries, but you may duplicate data and must manage the consequences (e.g., if Alice changes her email, and it’s embedded in old order documents, you may need to update it in multiple places, or decide you don’t care).
There’s no free lunch here — it’s an explicit modeling decision, not a strictly-better technology.
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
section: 5.5 5. Schema Flexibility: A Blessing and a Curse
text:
5.5 5. Schema Flexibility: A Blessing and a Curse
In a relational database, adding a column to a 10-million-row table requires an ALTER TABLE migration and some care. In MongoDB, you can insert a document with a new field at any time — the collection doesn’t complain.
For a statistician, the closest analogy is the difference between:

An R data.frame/tibble with fixed columns (relational table), versus
A list of lists, where each element can have different named entries (MongoDB collection).

# Relational-style: a data.frame, fixed columns
df <- data.frame(id = 1:2, name = c("Alice", "Bob"), age = c(30, NA))

# Document-style: a list of lists, heterogeneous structure
docs <- list(
  list(id = 1, name = "Alice", age = 30, hobbies = c("chess", "running")),
  list(id = 2, name = "Bob") # no age, no hobbies — and that's fine
)
This flexibility is genuinely useful when your data is naturally irregular (user-generated content, event logs with varying attributes, nested/hierarchical records). It’s a liability when you want the enforcement — e.g., you want the database itself to guarantee that age is always numeric, or that every document has an email. MongoDB does support optional schema validation rules, but they’re opt-in rather than the default posture of the system.
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
section: 5.6 6. Querying: dplyr/SQL Habits vs. MongoDB’s Query Language
text:
5.6 6. Querying: dplyr/SQL Habits vs. MongoDB’s Query Language
MongoDB queries are expressed as documents themselves (essentially, nested lists/JSON), which feels unusual at first if you’re used to SQL’s SELECT ... WHERE ... syntax or dplyr::filter().

5.6.1 Comparison table









Task
SQL
dplyr
MongoDB (shell syntax)




Filter rows
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount > 10
filter(orders, amount > 10)
db.orders.find({ amount: { $gt: 10 } })


Select columns
SELECT item, amount FROM orders
select(orders, item, amount)
db.orders.find({}, { item: 1, amount: 1 })


Sort
ORDER BY amount DESC
arrange(desc(amount))
.sort({ amount: -1 })


Group + aggregate
GROUP BY customer_id
group_by(customer_id) %>% summarise(...)
$group stage in an aggregation pipeline



MongoDB’s analogue to a SQL query with GROUP BY/joins/multiple transformations is the aggregation pipeline — a sequence of stages, each transforming the documents flowing through it, conceptually similar to chaining dplyr verbs with %>%:
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { amount: { $gt: 5 } } },       // like filter()
  { $group: { _id: "$customer_id",
              total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }, // like group_by() %>% summarise()
  { $sort: { total: -1 } }                   // like arrange(desc())
])
If you’re comfortable reading a dplyr pipe, the aggregation pipeline will feel more familiar than it first appears — it’s a sequence of verbs applied in order, just expressed as JSON stage objects instead of R function calls.
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
text:
5.7 7. Using MongoDB from R
You don’t have to leave R to work with MongoDB. The mongolite package provides a clean interface, and the workflow will feel close to what you already do with DBI.
install.packages("mongolite")
library(mongolite)

# Connect to a collection (analogous to opening a DBI connection to a table)
orders <- mongo(collection = "orders", db = "shop", url = "mongodb://localhost")

# Insert documents (rows) — takes a data.frame directly
orders$insert(data.frame(item = "Widget", amount = 9.99, customer_id = 1))

# Query and get a data.frame back — this is the key convenience
result <- orders$find('{"amount": {"$gt": 5}}')
head(result)

# Aggregation pipeline, expressed as a JSON string
pipeline <- '[
  {"$group": {"_id": "$customer_id", "total": {"$sum": "$amount"}}},
  {"$sort": {"total": -1}}
]'
summary_df <- orders$aggregate(pipeline)
Compare this to a typical relational workflow with DBI:
library(DBI)
library(RPostgres)

con <- dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), dbname = "shop")
result <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount > 5")
The big practical difference: mongolite queries and pipeline stages are written as JSON strings, not SQL strings — but the round trip (query in, tibble/data.frame out) is conceptually identical, which is good news for how much of your existing R workflow transfers.
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
section: 5.8 8. Consistency, Transactions, and Why This Matters to You
text:
5.8 8. Consistency, Transactions, and Why This Matters to You
Relational databases are traditionally built around ACID guarantees (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) — a transaction either fully happens or fully doesn’t, and the database enforces referential integrity via constraints.
Historically, NoSQL document stores traded some of these guarantees for scalability, often described (loosely) via the CAP theorem: in the presence of a network partition across distributed servers, a system must choose between Consistency (every read gets the latest write) and Availability (every request gets a response, possibly stale). Many early NoSQL systems leaned toward availability and “eventual consistency.”
Modern MongoDB has narrowed this gap substantially — it now supports multi-document ACID transactions — but the default mode of use, and the ecosystem’s design instincts, still favor flexible, denormalized, single-document operations over enforced cross-table integrity. If your work involves financial ledgers or anything where “the numbers must always add up, no exceptions, ever,” that’s traditionally been relational-database territory, and it’s worth understanding that this is a design lineage question, not just a feature checkbox — you can bolt strong consistency onto MongoDB, but it’s swimming against the current of how the system is typically used.
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
section: 5.9 9. When Each Approach Tends to Fit Better
text:
5.9 9. When Each Approach Tends to Fit Better







Favor relational (SQL) when…
Favor document (MongoDB) when…




Your data is naturally tabular and stable in structure
Your data is nested, hierarchical, or has varying fields per record


You need complex multi-table joins and strong referential integrity
You mostly fetch one entity plus its closely related data together


Strong consistency/transactions across entities is essential
High write/read throughput and horizontal scaling matter more


Your analysis workflow is fundamentally about tidy rectangular tables (which is common in statistics!)
Your data is closer to logs, events, user profiles, or content with irregular shape



For a lot of statistical work — clean, rectangular datasets destined for modeling — relational databases (or just flat files/data frames) remain a very natural fit, and you’ll often find yourself flattening MongoDB documents back into rectangular data frames before doing any actual analysis, since most statistical methods assume tidy, rectangular input.
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
section: 5.10 10. A Worked Mini-Example: Same Data, Both Ways
text:
5.10 10. A Worked Mini-Example: Same Data, Both Ways
Relational (two tables + a join):
CREATE TABLE customers (customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
  item TEXT,
  amount NUMERIC
);

SELECT c.name, o.item, o.amount
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Document (one collection, embedded):
library(mongolite)
customers <- mongo("customers", db = "shop")

customers$insert('{
  "_id": 1,
  "name": "Alice",
  "orders": [
    {"item": "Widget", "amount": 9.99},
    {"item": "Gadget", "amount": 19.99}
  ]
}')

# Pull it back out, then flatten to a data.frame for analysis
raw <- customers$find()
flat <- tidyr::unnest(raw, orders)
Notice the last line: even when working with MongoDB, you often end up reaching for tidyr::unnest() to get back to the rectangular shape you actually want for modeling. This is a common and completely normal pattern — document stores are often optimized for how an application writes and reads data, not for how a statistician wants to analyze it, and translating between the two is a routine part of the workflow.
crumbs: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians

title: 5  NoSQL and MongoDB: An Introduction for Statisticians
text:
5.11 11. Summary

MongoDB stores flexible, JSON-like documents in collections, instead of enforcing rows-in-tables with a fixed schema.
The relational instinct to normalize is replaced by a document instinct to denormalize/embed, optimized around how the data will be read.
Querying feels different syntactically (JSON-shaped queries, aggregation pipelines) but maps conceptually onto SQL/dplyr verbs you already know.
Consistency and transactional guarantees are available in modern MongoDB but aren’t the system’s traditional default posture the way they are in relational databases.
For statistical analysis specifically, you’ll frequently pull data out of MongoDB and flatten it back into rectangular form — so document databases are often best understood as an operational/application-layer tool, with relational-style rectangular data as the destination for actual modeling.

If you want to go deeper next, worthwhile follow-ups are: MongoDB’s aggregation pipeline in more depth, schema validation rules, and how sharding/replication work for horizontal scaling.

6.1 What you’ll need
It’s written against the AI Incident Database schema, so the field names below match what you’ll actually see, but the thinking process, how to read a pipeline, how to build a new one from scratch, how to avoid downloading more than you need, carries over to any MongoDB collection you work with.
Install the packages you’ll need once, up front:
mongolite is the simplest way to talk to MongoDB from R, and it hands data back as a data frame, which is exactly the shape tidyverse tools expect. Both $find() (simple queries) and $aggregate() (multi-stage pipelines) live on the connection object it gives you.

title: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis
section: 6.2 Know your collections before you query
text:
6.2 Know your collections before you query
The schema you’ve been given defines several collections. The two you’ll care about most are:

reports — the actual documents/articles. This is where the free text lives. Key fields:

_id (objectId), report_number (number) — report_number is the human-friendly key used to link a report to the incident(s) it belongs to
title, text, plain_text — text may retain markdown/HTML formatting from the original source; plain_text is the cleaned version and is almost always what you want for tokenising/sentiment work
description — a short editor-written summary, separate from the report body
authors, submitters — arrays of strings
tags — array of free-text tags
language, source_domain, url
date_published, date_submitted, date_downloaded, date_modified
embedding — a precomputed vector embedding of the text (nested object with a vector field); large, and you generally won’t need it unless you’re doing similarity/clustering work directly on the provided vectors
is_incident_report (boolean)

incidents — the higher-level “event” that one or more reports are describing. Key fields:

_id (objectId), incident_id (number)
title, description, date
reports — an array of report_number values (not full documents) pointing back into the reports collection — this is how you join the two collections
Alleged deployer of AI system, Alleged developer of AI system, Alleged harmed or nearly harmed parties — arrays of entity-name strings
implicated_systems — array of strings
editors, editor_notes

classifications — tagging/label data (an attributes field) that links back to incidents/reports by their IDs — useful if you want to bring in categorical labels alongside the report text.
entities — a lookup table of named entities (entity_id, name) referenced by the “alleged deployer/developer/harmed parties” fields above.

For most text-analysis tasks, you’ll mainly work with reports.plain_text, optionally joined to incidents for grouping/labels — which is exactly the join used as the worked example throughout this sheet.

title: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis
text:
6.3 Connecting to the cluster
Never hard-code your username and password directly into a script you might commit to GitHub or share with teammates. Use an .Renviron file instead.
Create/edit your .Renviron file (run this once):
usethis::edit_r_environ()
Add a line like this, save, and restart R:
MONGO_URI="mongodb+srv://myusername:mypassword@ai-incident-database.ugkyb5n.mongodb.net/"
Now connect from your script — one connection object per collection:
library(mongolite)

db_name <- "aiidprod"

reports_conn <- mongo(collection = "reports", db = db_name,
                       url = Sys.getenv("MONGO_URI"))

incidents_conn <- mongo(collection = "incidents", db = db_name,
                         url = Sys.getenv("MONGO_URI"))

# quick sanity check
reports_conn$count()
incidents_conn$count()
If $count() returns a number rather than an error, you’re connected. This number is also your first data-volume signal.

title: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis
section: 6.4 The core mental model: pipelines are JSON, R is the courier
text:
6.4 The core mental model: pipelines are JSON, R is the courier
$aggregate() sends a pipeline to MongoDB’s aggregation engine and gets back a data frame. The key thing to internalize: the pipeline itself is not R code — it’s JSON. You’re writing MongoDB’s own query language as a string, and R is just the courier. That means:

Field names are quoted strings ("report_number"), not R symbols.
$ in front of a name ("$incident") means “the value of this field,” not an R accessor.
The whole thing is an array ([ ... ]) of stage objects ({ ... }), executed top to bottom.

Think of a pipeline as an assembly line: each stage receives the documents from the stage before it, transforms them, and passes the result to the next stage. Nothing is “queried” all at once — it’s a sequence of transformations.
pipeline <- '[ ... ]'   # a JSON array, written as an R string

reports_with_incident <- reports_conn$aggregate(pipeline) |>
  tibble::as_tibble()
crumbs: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis

title: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis
text:
6.5 Don’t download the whole collection
It’s easy to fall into this pattern:
library(tidyverse)

report_cols <- '{
    "_id": 1, "report_number": 1, "title": 1, "plain_text": 1,
    "description": 1, "tags": 1, "authors": 1, "language": 1,
    "source_domain": 1, "date_published": 1
  }'

reports <- reports_conn$find(fields = report_cols) |> as_tibble()

glimpse(reports)
Notice what this does: $find() with no query argument means “give me every document in the collection.” fields trims the columns, but it does nothing to trim the rows — you’re still pulling every document over the network and materializing it in R’s memory before you’ve filtered, grouped, or summarized anything. On a small collection this is harmless. On a collection with hundreds of thousands of documents (especially ones with a plain_text field, which tends to be large — or an embedding field, which is a full numeric vector per document), it’s the single most common source of slow, memory-hungry R/Mongo scripts.
The general rule: MongoDB is a database with its own query and aggregation engine — use it as one. Only bring rows into R once they’re already filtered, grouped, or reduced to roughly the size you actually need for the next step.

6.5.1 Filter rows on the server with query
$find() takes a query argument (the same JSON $match-style filter used in aggregation):
# Downloads everything, then filters in R — avoid this
reports <- reports_conn$find(fields = report_cols) |> as_tibble()
recent  <- reports |> filter(date_published >= as.Date("2023-01-01"))

# Filters on the server, only recent documents cross the network
query <- '{ "date_published": { "$gte": { "$date": "2023-01-01T00:00:00Z" } } }'
recent <- reports_conn$find(query = query, fields = report_cols) |> as_tibble()

# Also useful: language filter, straight from mongolite's query syntax
reports_en <- reports_conn$find(
  query  = '{"language": "en"}',
  fields = '{"_id": 1, "report_number": 1, "title": 1, "plain_text": 1}'
) |> as_tibble()
For the full query syntax mongolite supports, see https://jeroen.github.io/mongolite/query-data.html#query-syntax.


6.5.2 Let $group summarize before it ever reaches R
If your end goal is a summary (counts, averages, distinct values), don’t pull raw rows into dplyr::group_by() |> summarize(). Do the equivalent with $group in an aggregation pipeline, so only the summary — not the underlying documents — travels over the wire:
pipeline <- '[
  { "$match":   { "language": "en" } },
  { "$group":   { "_id": "$source_domain", "n": { "$sum": 1 } } },
  { "$sort":    { "n": -1 } },
  { "$limit":   20 }
]'

top_domains <- reports_conn$aggregate(pipeline) |> as_tibble()
This never materializes the full reports collection anywhere — Mongo does the counting, and R receives 20 rows. The date_published year-grouping example below follows the same idea:
reports_per_year <- reports_conn$aggregate('[
  { "$group": {
      "_id": { "$substr": ["$date_published", 0, 4] },
      "n": { "$sum": 1 }
  }},
  { "$sort": { "_id": 1 } }
]') |> as_tibble()


6.5.3 Count before you fetch
Before running any $find()/$aggregate() without a filter, get a sense of scale first:
reports_conn$count()                             # whole collection
reports_conn$count('{ "language": "en" }')        # a filtered subset
If that number is larger than you’re comfortable holding in memory (as a rough guide: tens of thousands of documents with large text fields), that’s your signal to filter further, project fewer fields, or move to the batching approach in 8.5.


6.5.4 limit, skip, and $sample for peeking or paging
# Peek at a handful of documents without downloading the rest
sample_reports <- reports_conn$find(fields = report_cols, limit = 100) |> as_tibble()

# Manual pagination
page <- reports_conn$find(fields = report_cols, limit = 500, skip = 1000) |> as_tibble()
For a genuinely random sample (not just “the first N”), use $sample in an aggregation pipeline instead of limit, since find(limit = ...) returns documents in storage order, not a random subset:
pipeline <- '[ { "$sample": { "size": 500 } } ]'
random_sample <- reports_conn$aggregate(pipeline) |> as_tibble()


6.5.5 A decision guide







Your goal
Reach for




A quick look at the data’s shape
find(limit = ...) or $sample


Rows matching a condition
find(query = ...) or an aggregation $match


A summary/aggregate statistic
An aggregation pipeline with $group — never raw rows into dplyr::summarize()


A join across collections, summarized
$lookup → $unwind → $group inside one pipeline


Every document, but too many to hold at once
$iterate() with batching


“How big is this even going to be?”
$count() first, always, before an unfiltered $find()/$aggregate()

title: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis
section: 6.6 A worked pipeline, stage by stage: joining reports to incidents
text:
6.6 A worked pipeline, stage by stage: joining reports to incidents
This is the actual join you’ll want for this schema — reports linked to the incident(s) that reference them by report_number.
pipeline <- '[
  {
    "$lookup": {
      "from": "incidents",
      "localField": "report_number",
      "foreignField": "reports",
      "as": "incident"
    }
  },
  {
    "$unwind": {
      "path": "$incident",
      "preserveNullAndEmptyArrays": true
    }
  },
  {
    "$project": {
      "_id": 1,
      "report_number": 1,
      "title": 1,
      "plain_text": 1,
      "description": 1,
      "tags": 1,
      "authors": 1,
      "language": 1,
      "source_domain": 1,
      "date_published": 1,

      "incident_id": "$incident.incident_id",
      "incident_title": "$incident.title",
      "date": "$incident.date"
    }
  }
]'

reports_with_incident <- reports_conn$aggregate(pipeline) |>
  tibble::as_tibble()

6.6.1 Stage 1 — $lookup (a SQL-style JOIN)
For every document in reports, MongoDB looks in the incidents collection for documents where incidents.reports matches this document’s report_number. All matches are attached as an array under a new field called incident.
Mental model: “For each report, go fetch related incidents and staple them on as a list.”


6.6.2 Stage 2 — $unwind (flatten the array)
$lookup always produces an array, even if there’s exactly one match. $unwind explodes that array so each matched element becomes its own document (one report + one incident, instead of one report + an array of incidents). If a report matched 3 incidents, $unwind turns 1 document into 3.
preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true is important — without it, reports with no matching incident would be silently dropped from the results. With it, they’re kept, with incident set to null. Whether you want this depends on whether you’re doing an inner join (drop unmatched) or a left join (keep unmatched) mentally.


6.6.3 Stage 3 — $project (reshape the output)

"field": 1 means “keep this field, unchanged.”
"new_name": "$path.to.value" means “create a field called new_name, populated from this path.” Since $unwind turned incident into a single embedded object (not an array), you can reach into it with dot notation ($incident.incident_id).

This last step is why the whole pipeline exists: $lookup + $unwind get the related data attached, and $project flattens it into a clean, tibble-friendly shape — no nested lists left for R to deal with.
crumbs: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis

title: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis
section: 6.7 The general thinking process for writing a new pipeline
text:
6.7 The general thinking process for writing a new pipeline
Before writing any JSON, answer these in plain English:

What’s my starting collection, and what’s the shape of one document in it?
What do I want one row of my final output to represent? (One report? One report-incident pair? One tag with a count?)
What has to happen to get from (1) to (2)? — usually some combination of: bring in related data, filter out documents, reshape/rename fields, flatten arrays, or summarize groups.

Each of those verbs maps to a specific stage. Once you can state the transformation in English, the JSON is just translation:








You want to…
Stage
Notes




Join in data from another collection
$lookup
Always produces an array field


Flatten an array field (incl. $lookup results)
$unwind
Use preserveNullAndEmptyArrays deliberately


Filter documents (like SQL WHERE)
$match
Put this as early as possible for performance


Choose/rename/compute output fields
$project
1 keeps, 0 excludes, "$field" copies/renames


Add new fields without dropping others
$addFields / $set
Like $project but additive — you don’t have to relist every field


Group and summarize (SQL GROUP BY)
$group
_id is the grouping key; use $sum, $avg, $push, etc. as accumulators


Sort results
$sort
1 ascending, -1 descending


Limit / skip (pagination)
$limit, $skip
Cheapest late in the pipeline, after filtering


Count documents
$count
Collapses everything into { "count": N }


Random sample of documents
$sample
Use instead of limit when you want a true random subset


Run several sub-pipelines and combine
$facet
Useful for “give me totals AND a filtered list” in one round trip


Reshape a document to become one of its subfields
$replaceRoot / $replaceWith
Common after $unwind when you only want the nested object


Traverse a hierarchy/graph (e.g. org charts)
$graphLookup
Recursive $lookup




6.7.1 Worked example: $match + $group from scratch
Say you want: “For each source_domain, how many reports were published, restricted to reports published after 2020?”
Walk through the three questions:

Starting collection: reports, each document is one report.
Desired output row: one row per source_domain, with a count.
Transformation: filter by date, then group by domain and count.

pipeline <- '[
  {
    "$match": {
      "date_published": { "$gte": { "$date": "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z" } }
    }
  },
  {
    "$group": {
      "_id": "$source_domain",
      "n_reports": { "$sum": 1 }
    }
  },
  {
    "$sort": { "n_reports": -1 }
  }
]'

report_counts <- reports_conn$aggregate(pipeline) |> tibble::as_tibble()
Notice the pattern repeats: filter/join stages first, reshape stages last. $match should almost always come as early as possible (it reduces the document count before any expensive work), and $project/$group/$sort come afterward to shape the final result.

title: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis
text:
7.3 Debugging and building pipelines incrementally

Build incrementally. Write one stage, run $aggregate(), inspect the output, then add the next stage. Debugging a 5-stage pipeline all at once is much harder than debugging it one stage at a time.
Comment out stages by truncating the array. Since the pipeline is just a string, you can test '[ stage1 ]', then '[ stage1, stage2 ]', and so on.
Watch for the array-vs-object trap. After $lookup, a field is an array. After $unwind, that same field is a single object. Referencing $incident.title only works after unwinding (or if you know there’s exactly one match and use $arrayElemAt).
Use jsonlite::toJSON()/fromJSON() to build pipelines as R lists instead of raw strings, if you find quoting JSON by hand error-prone:
pipeline_list <- list(
  list(`$match` = list(date_published = list(`$gte` = "2020-01-01"))),
  list(`$group` = list(`_id` = "$source_domain", n_reports = list(`$sum` = 1)))
)
pipeline <- jsonlite::toJSON(pipeline_list, auto_unbox = TRUE)
This trades JSON-string fiddliness for R’s backtick-quoted-name syntax (`$match`) — pick whichever you find less error-prone. Many R/Mongo users stick with raw JSON strings for anything beyond 2–3 stages, since MongoDB’s own documentation and the shell both use JSON, so the translation from “docs example” to “your pipeline” stays literal.
preserveNullAndEmptyArrays is a decision, not a default. Always ask explicitly: do I want to drop documents with no match, or keep them with null?
Field order in $project doesn’t matter to Mongo, but keeping it consistent with your intended output column order makes the resulting tibble easier to read.
Test aggregations in MongoDB Compass or mongosh first, if you have access — it’s faster to iterate there and then paste the finished JSON into your R string than to round-trip through R for every tweak.

title: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis
text:
7.5 Common pitfalls

Connection refused / timeout — your IP isn’t allow-listed in Atlas Network Access, or you’re on a network (uni wifi, VPN) that blocks the MongoDB port. Test the connection before you need it.
Pulling embedding by accident — it’s a full numeric vector per document; leave it out of your fields projection unless you specifically need it, or your find() calls will be slow and memory-heavy.
Using text instead of plain_text — text can retain markdown/HTML from the original source, which will pollute your tokens (<, ##, href=, etc.). Prefer plain_text for tokenising.
unnest_wider() on the wrong field — authors, tags, and the “alleged parties” fields are arrays of strings, so they need unnest_longer(). unnest_wider() is for fields that are nested objects (there aren’t many of those in reports/incidents).
Joining incidents to reports on the wrong key — incidents.reports holds report_number values, not _id (objectId) values. Join on report_number, not _id.
Encoding issues (garbled characters) — check Encoding() on your text column and re-encode with iconv() if you see mojibake.
Credentials in scripts — always use Sys.getenv() against an .Renviron file, never paste the connection string directly into a script you’ll share or commit.
Downloading before filtering/summarizing — the most common source of slow, memory-heavy scripts against this collection specifically; before writing an unfiltered find()/aggregate().

7.6.1 Pipeline stages
The short version: $match/$lookup early, $project/$group/$sort/$limit late.


7.6.2 Package cheat sheet

title: 6  MongoDB Atlas to R: Connecting, Pipelines, and Text Analysis
text:
7.7 Summary checklists
Writing any new pipeline

State in one sentence what one output row should represent.
List the stages needed to get there, in order (join → filter → flatten → reshape → group → sort → limit).
Write and test one stage at a time.
Put $match as early as possible; put $sort/$limit as late as possible.
After any $lookup, decide immediately whether you need $unwind, and whether unmatched documents should be kept.
Finish with $project (or $set) so the shape handed to tibble::as_tibble() is already flat and clean.
Before any unfiltered find()/aggregate(), run $count() first.

Size-conscious tidyverse/text-mining work

Ask what the smallest result is that answers your question — a count? a top-20 list? — and try to get MongoDB to produce that directly.
Exclude large fields (plain_text, description, embedding) from fields/$project unless this specific step needs them.
Filter (query/$match) and, for exploration, sample ($sample) before tokenizing.
Prefer $group/$addFields for summaries over pulling raw rows into dplyr::summarize() or unnest_tokens().
If you must touch the full corpus, batch with $iterate() and combine only small, already-summarized pieces — never accumulate raw batches into one growing tibble.

Good luck with the competition.

title: 7  Data dictionary for AI Incident Database
text:
7.1 Overview
At a high level, the collections fall into three groups:
Each collection section below lists field name, inferred type, and a description. Types marked array<T> denote an array whose elements are of type T; a bare array means an empty array was observed and no element type could be inferred. object{...} denotes an embedded sub-document, with its own fields described inline or in a nested table.
crumbs: 7  Data dictionary for AI Incident Database

title: 7  Data dictionary for AI Incident Database
text:
Core record collections: incidents, reports, entities, entity_relationships are the canonical, published data users browse in the “Discover” app.
Classification collections: taxa, classifications are the flexible, namespaced taxonomy system used to tag incidents/reports (e.g. the CSET taxonomy).
Workflow / pipeline collections: submissions, candidates quickadd, duplicates, entity_duplicates, incident_links, checklists, migrations are there to support the editorial pipeline that turns a scraped news article into a published incident, plus ancillary tools.
crumbs: 7  Data dictionary for AI Incident Database

title: 7  Data dictionary for AI Incident Database
text:
7.2 Core record collections

7.2.1 incidents
The canonical, published incident records which are the primary entity of the database. Each incident aggregates one or more reports.








Field
Type
Description




_id
objectId
MongoDB primary key.


incident_id
number
Public, human-facing incident number (used in URLs like /cite/123).


title
string
Short incident title shown in listings.


description
string
Editor-written summary of the incident.


date
string
Date the incident occurred (YYYY-MM-DD).


reports
array<number>
report_numbers of the reports that make up this incident.


editors
array<string>
Identifiers/usernames of editors who have contributed to the record.


editor_notes
string
Free-text internal notes for editors.


implicated_systems
array<string>
entity_ids of the AI system(s) implicated.


Alleged deployer of AI system / AllegedDeployerOfAISystem
array<string>
entity_ids of the party alleged to have deployed the system. Both the legacy space-separated key and a camelCase duplicate are present; the camelCase versions were added because MongoDB Atlas App Services/Realm (_id__baas_transaction, see below) cannot use field names containing spaces in GraphQL.


Alleged developer of AI system / AllegedDeveloperOfAISystem
array<string>
entity_ids of the party alleged to have developed the system (same legacy/camelCase pairing as above).


Alleged harmed or nearly harmed parties / AllegedHarmedOrNearlyHarmedParties
array<string>
entity_ids of parties alleged to have been harmed or nearly harmed.


nlp_similar_incidents
array<object>
NLP-generated recommendations of related incidents: {incident_id, similarity}.


editor_similar_incidents
array<number>
Incident IDs an editor has manually confirmed as similar.


editor_dissimilar_incidents
array<number>
Incident IDs an editor has manually marked as not similar (overrides NLP suggestions).


flagged_dissimilar_incidents
array<number>
Incident IDs flagged by users/editors for review as likely-incorrect similarity matches.


embedding
object<br>{vector, from_reports}
Text embedding vector representing the incident, plus the report_numbers it was derived from. Powers similarity search and the spatial view.

title: 7  Data dictionary for AI Incident Database
text:
7.5 Notes on schema conventions

Legacy/camelCase field pairs. A few incidents fields exist twice — once with spaces (e.g. Alleged deployer of AI system) and once in camelCase (AllegedDeployerOfAISystem). The camelCase versions exist because MongoDB Atlas App Services’ GraphQL layer cannot expose field names containing spaces; both are kept in sync for backward compatibility.
array with no element type. Where the scan reports a bare array alongside a more specific array<T> for the same field, it simply means some documents had an empty array for that field, so no element type could be inferred from them.
Embeddings. embedding.vector fields store dense vector representations of text (incident/report/candidate content) used for nearest-neighbor similarity search and clustering (e.g. tsne for 2-D visualization). from_text_hash / from_reports record what the embedding was computed from, so it can be invalidated and recomputed when the source text changes.
Namespacing. The taxonomy system (taxa + classifications) is deliberately pluralistic: multiple organizations can define their own namespace (e.g. a general taxonomy alongside domain-specific ones) and apply independent classifications to the same incidents, rather than the database enforcing one canonical taxonomy.

Text mining is a means to an analytical insight, not the insight itself. A clear tf-idf or sentiment analysis tied to a specific question scores better than a kitchen-sink pipeline with no narrative tying it together.

title: 9  Good Visualisation & Tables
text:
NoteWhy this matters



Analysis & Evidence (35 points) and Report Clarity & Storytelling (20 points) — more than half of your score comes from these elements, so it’s worth looking over these materials to create good visualisation and tables. Even solid analysis loses marks if it’s shown as raw R output or a cluttered default chart.


Start from the message, not the chart: write the one-sentence finding first, then pick the plot or table that makes it obvious. A few things worth knowing regardless of which chart you pick, position and length (bar charts, scatter plots) are judged far more accurately than angle and area (pie charts), so prefer the former; sort categories by value instead of leaving them alphabetical; and for tables, don’t paste a summary() printout into the report, broom::tidy() turns a fitted model into a data frame, and gtsummary::tbl_regression() turns that into a table you can actually trim down to what answers your question.
For the full treatment, perception, colour palettes, a worked diagnose/redesign/evaluate example, and table-formatting details, go through the two Monash ETC5523 (Communicating with Data) lectures this is drawn from:

Week 5 — from model outputs to communicative tables
Week 6 — effective data visualisation
